stories.title: Law Firm Greenberg Traurig Takes 25K SF at Related Ross Dev in West Palm
stories.excerpt: Law firm Greenberg Traurig is relocating to another Related Ross building in Downtown West Palm Beach, Fla. The firm signed a 10-year lease to occupy about 25,000 square feet at the 15 CityPlace office development, which remains under construction, the tenant announced. The deal spans the entire 12th floor of the 25-story project. Move-in is scheduled for fall 2027. “The move reflects our long-term commitment to the West Palm Beach market and positions us to meet increasing client demand throughout Palm Beach County and beyond,” Tracy Gerber, co-managing shareholder of Greenberg Traurig’s West Palm Beach office, said in a statement. 15 CityPlace, and the neighboring 10 CityPlace, are expected to be completed next year after developer Related Ross secured a $772 million construction debt package last year. Health care provider Cleveland Clinic has already pre-leased 125,000 square feet at 15 CityPlace, which will span about 500,000 square feet. The law firm is currently stationed at Philips Point, where it leases roughly 30,000 square feet. Related Ross, led by Stephen Ross, purchased the 448,914-square-foot office for $282 million in 2021. The two-building complex, which dates back to 1985, is currently undergoing a $120 million renovation. Even as Greenberg Traurig departs, the building has nabbed new tenants: global index provider MSCI taking 7,500 square feet, investment bank Solomon Partners taking 4,200 square feet, and Integrity Pro Consulting taking 1,300 square feet. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Greenberg Traurig signs 25K SF lease at Related Ross's 15 CityPlace, West Palm Beach; move-in fall 2027.
Cleveland Clinic pre-leased 125K SF at same building; 15 CityPlace backed by $772M construction debt.
Law firm cites 'increasing client demand throughout Palm Beach County' as driver of long-term commitment.
stories.summary: Greenberg Traurig has committed to a 10-year, 25,000-sf lease at the 15 CityPlace office tower in Downtown West Palm Beach, with move-in scheduled for fall 2027. The deal spans an entire floor of the 25-story mixed-use project, which is under construction and already anchored by Cleveland Clinic's 125,000-sf pre-lease. Related Ross financed the $500M+ project with a $772M construction loan closed last year.
stories.impact: Large professional services and healthcare anchor tenants signing long-term leases on future office supply signals robust employment and services sector growth in West Palm Beach. Multifamily developers should track job creation and income growth in Palm Beach County; rising professional/healthcare employment typically precedes demand for workforce housing. Strong pre-leasing in new Class A office increases likelihood of on-time delivery and could accelerate mixed-use amenity demand in the submarket.

stories.title: Talonvest Closes Refi for Two-Hotel Sunnyvale Campus
stories.excerpt: Talonvest Capital closed a $105,000,000 refinancing for a two-hotel campus in Sunnyvale on behalf of K1 Dev, LLC, an entity controlled by T2 Hospitality, a vertically integrated hospitality real estate investment and development company. The properties include the 186-key TETRA Hotel, Autograph Collection, and the 164-key AC Hotel by Marriott Sunnyvale Moffett Park. The refinancing consists of a non-recourse bridge loan structured with a three-year initial term and two one-year extension options. Talonvest secured favorable terms and substantial interest savings over the full five-year loan term. Jeff Miller, Kim Bishop, Will Hainlen, Carson Kurland, and Lauren Maehler were among the Talonvest team members responsible for arranging the financing. Nayiri Madenlian, CFO of T2 Hospitality, commented, “Working with the Talonvest team was an exceptional experience. They added meaningful value at every stage of the process, and their execution made this the best broker experience we’ve had over many years of financing.” The post Talonvest Closes Refi for Two-Hotel Sunnyvale Campus appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Talonvest arranges $105M refi for two-hotel campus in Sunnyvale (186-key TETRA Hotel, 164-key AC Hotel).
Non-recourse bridge loan; three-year initial term plus two one-year extensions; favorable terms secured.
Sunnyvale Moffett Park submarket showing hospitality asset stability and refinancing appetite.
stories.summary: Talonvest Capital closed a $105M refinancing for K1 Dev/T2 Hospitality's two-hotel campus in Sunnyvale comprising the 186-key TETRA Hotel Autograph Collection and 164-key AC Hotel by Marriott Sunnyvale Moffett Park. The non-recourse bridge loan carries a three-year initial term with two one-year extension options and secured favorable terms and interest savings over the five-year loan horizon.
stories.impact: Hospitality asset refi activity in Silicon Valley submarkets (Sunnyvale/Moffett Park) reflects confidence in Bay Area travel and corporate demand recovery. However, multifamily developers should note that tech sector volatility and work-from-home trends continue to dampen office and transient worker housing demand in this region; focus should remain on essential service worker and lower-income renter bases.

stories.title: Law Firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee Leases 11K SF at 7 World Trade Center
stories.excerpt: Washington D.C.-based law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee is establishing a new office in New York City. The firm, which specializes in high stakes trials, investigations and crisis management, has inked an 11,167-square-foot lease on the 34th floor of 7 World Trade Center, developer and landlord Silverstein Properties announced Monday. Silverstein did not disclose the length of the lease or the asking rent. However, a source close to the deal noted asking rents in the building range from $100 to $150 per square foot. “We are excited to welcome our teams and our clients into our new Manhattan office later this year,” Jeannie Rhee, managing partner of Dunn Isaacson Rhee, said in a statement. “7 World Trade Center offers the ideal combination of thoughtful design, functionality, and a premier location in the heart of the Financial District and a stone’s throw to the Southern District of New York courthouse.” Dunn Isaacson Rhee will relocate from 11 Park Place, also in the Financial District. It’s unclear when the firm will make the move. Dunn Isaacson Rhee did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Lisa Ann Pollakowski, Cory Gahr and Richard Plehn from Lee & Associates represented the tenant in the deal, while Silverstein was represented in-house by Keith A. Cody, Gordon Hough and Harlan Strader, as well as by CBRE’s MaryAnn Tighe. Lee & Associates did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. “Dunn Isaacson Rhee represents the caliber of organization that continues to define 7 World Trade Center as one of Downtown Manhattan’s premier office destinations,” Silverstein’s Cody said in a statement. “Today’s leading firms are seeking workplaces that reflect their brand, support their people and provide an exceptional experience for their clients. bullets: DC law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee leases 11.2K SF at 7 World Trade Center, Manhattan; asking rent $100–$150/sf.
Firm relocating within Financial District; move-in later in 2024; cite proximity to Southern District courthouse.
Silverstein Properties development showing continued office leasing momentum in Downtown Manhattan.
stories.summary: Washington D.C.-based law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee signed an 11,167-sf lease on the 34th floor of Silverstein Properties' 7 World Trade Center in Manhattan's Financial District. The asking rent range is $100–$150 per square foot; the firm is relocating from 11 Park Place, also in the Financial District, to gain proximity to the Southern District courthouse.
stories.impact: Professional services tenant expansions in Lower Manhattan/Financial District continue post-pandemic recovery in office leasing. Multifamily developers should note that robust law firm and finance sector anchoring supports service worker and upper-income renter demand in adjacent neighborhoods; however, this office traction is concentrated in prime Class A buildings and should not mask broader softness in secondary Manhattan office markets.

stories.title: Boston Sees Building Boom in Subsidized Housing
stories.excerpt: The City of Boston put much of its $560 million in pandemic-era relief funds into building housing. As a result, Boston has seen more than 6,200 new income-restricted units built or under construction during Mayor Michelle Wu’s first term, the highest level of production in the past 25 years, according to a new report from the city’s Office of Housing. The city also has a higher percentage of subsidized housing inventory than any of its peers in the nation’s 15 largest markets. The Boston Business Journal reported that the spike in new subsidized homes comes as construction has slowed more broadly in Boston, coinciding with rising construction costs and higher interest rates. However, the federal government’s pandemic aid to the city of Boston is set to dry up by year’s end, the Business Journal reported. Accordingly, Boston now seeks new funding avenues, Karina Oliver-Milchman, director of policy development and research for theOffice of Housing, told the Business Journal. The post Boston Sees Building Boom in Subsidized Housing appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Boston built 6,200+ income-restricted units in past 25 years; highest production during Mayor Wu's first term.
City deployed $560M pandemic relief funds into subsidized housing; federal aid expires end-of-year.
Rising construction costs and higher interest rates slowing broader Boston housing production.
stories.summary: Boston has delivered more than 6,200 income-restricted units built or under construction over the past 25 years, with the highest production surge during Mayor Michelle Wu's first term, driven by deployment of $560M in federal pandemic relief. The city now holds a higher percentage of subsidized housing than any peer in the nation's 15 largest markets. However, federal pandemic aid is set to dry up by year-end, and the city faces slowing broader construction amid rising costs and interest rates.
stories.impact: Surge in subsidized unit production in Boston crowd-sourced government capital and compressed market-rate multifamily supply and demand signals. As federal stimulus expires end-of-2024, expect sharp deceleration in Boston-area apartment starts; market-rate developers should position acquisitions and underwriting for higher cap rates and tighter construction timelines. Conversely, investor appetite for deed-restricted assets may soften as subsidy sources dry up, creating exit risk for recent affordable housing developments.

stories.title: SRS Real Estate Partners Completes Sale of Grocery Property in Michigan
stories.excerpt: SRS Real Estate Partners has completed the $6.92 million sale of a single-tenant grocery property located at 2103 Parkview Avenue in Kalamazoo, Michigan. The 29,000-square-foot freestanding grocery property is situated on 2.33 acres and is occupied by D&W Fresh Market, operated by a subsidiary of C&S Wholesale, under a corporate-guaranteed absolute triple net lease. Originally built in 1955, the property has a current lease extending through 2031, with approximately five years remaining, and includes three five-year renewal options.SRS Capital Markets Senior Vice President Jeff Gates represented the seller, a Toronto-based investor group. The buyer was an institutional investor. “Single-tenant grocery properties continue to be among the most sought-after net lease investments due to their ability to generate durable cash flow and perform well across economic cycles,” said Gates. Located along Parkview Avenue in one of Kalamazoo’s primary retail corridors, the property is surrounded by a strong mix of national retailers and restaurants. The post SRS Real Estate Partners Completes Sale of Grocery Property in Michigan appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: SRS Real Estate Partners sold $6.92M single-tenant grocery property (D&W Fresh Market) in Kalamazoo, Michigan.
29K SF property on 2.33 acres; lease through 2031 with three five-year renewal options; absolute triple-net.
Buyer: institutional investor; seller: Toronto-based investor group.
stories.summary: SRS Real Estate Partners brokered the $6.92M sale of a 29,000-sf single-tenant grocery property at 2103 Parkview Avenue in Kalamazoo, Michigan. The property is occupied by D&W Fresh Market under a corporate-guaranteed absolute triple-net lease extending through 2031, with approximately five years remaining and three five-year renewal options. An institutional investor acquired the asset from a Toronto-based seller.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. Single-tenant net-lease grocery sales are institutional cap-rate plays and do not signal shifts in Kalamazoo residential demand or supply. Multifamily developers should monitor grocery/retail anchor stability in target secondary markets as a proxy for neighborhood economic health, but this transaction alone carries minimal implications for apartment development.

stories.title: Gantry Secures $31M for Kansas City Warehouse Facility
stories.excerpt: Gantry has secured a $30.5 million permanent loan to refinance maturing debt for a 603,000-square-foot warehouse facility located in the Skyport Industrial Center at 7501 NW 106th Terrace in Kansas City’s Northland submarket. The multi-tenant facility underwent a full renovation in 2023 and is now 100%-leased in a multi-tenant format for a range of logistics uses. Building specs include 32’ clear heights, 22,000-square-foot bay size, 135’ deep truck court, cross-dock expansion capacity, and ready access to regional and national logistics infrastructure, including Kansas City International Airport, I-29 and I-435. Gantry’s Mark Reichter, Principal, with the firm’s Kansas City production office, represented the borrower, a private real estate investor. The seven-year, fixed-rate, non-recourse loan was secured through one of Gantry’s correspondent life company lenders and includes one year of interest-only payments, followed by 30-year amortization. Gantry will service the loan for the lender. bullets: Gantry secured $30.5M permanent loan to refi warehouse facility in Kansas City Northland (Skyport Industrial Center).
603K SF, 100% leased, multi-tenant logistics; full 2023 renovation; 32' clear heights, ready for cross-dock.
Seven-year fixed-rate non-recourse loan; one-year interest-only; 30-year amortization; life company lender.
stories.summary: Gantry arranged a $30.5M permanent refinancing loan for a 603,000-sf, fully-leased multi-tenant warehouse facility in Kansas City's Northland submarket (Skyport Industrial Center). The asset was fully renovated in 2023 and features logistics-optimized specs (32' clear heights, 22K-sf bays, 135' truck court, cross-dock expansion). The seven-year fixed-rate, non-recourse loan includes one year of interest-only followed by 30-year amortization.
stories.impact: Robust industrial debt availability in Kansas City reflects strong regional logistics demand tied to I-29/I-435 corridor and airport proximity. Multifamily developers should note that industrial expansion and logistics employment growth in Kansas City Northland supports warehouse worker and essential services renter demand; co-location of industrial and residential development in secondary markets increasingly valuable for workforce housing.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Facilitates Sale of Grand Rapids MOB Property
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap announced the sale of East Paris Medical Center, a 10,011-square-foot, three-suite medical and professional office in Grand Rapids, Michigan. The property sold for $2.13 million.“Investors were drawn to the property’s strong location and future upside potential, with all tenants currently paying at or below market rents,” said Seth Haron, managing director of investments. Haron, Ashish Vakhariya and Darin Gross, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s Detroit office, had the exclusive listing to market the property on behalf of the seller, a local private investor and retired physician.East Paris Medical Center is located at 1155 E. Paris Ave. S.E. along one of Grand Rapids’ most active healthcare corridors. The fully leased property is anchored by Trinity Health Michigan and is surrounded by major healthcare providers, including Corewell Health Blodgett Hospital, Corewell Health Butterworth Hospital and Trinity Health Grand Rapids Hospital. The post Marcus & Millichap Facilitates Sale of Grand Rapids MOB Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap facilitated sale of East Paris Medical Center in Grand Rapids, Michigan for $2.13M.
10K SF, three-suite medical/professional office; tenants paying at or below market rents.
Property sold by local private investor; buyer drawn to strong location and upside potential.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap brokered the sale of East Paris Medical Center, a 10,011-sf, three-suite medical and professional office building in Grand Rapids, Michigan, for $2.13M. All tenants were paying at or below market rents, which was cited as a draw for the buyer's upside potential. The property was marketed by the firm's Detroit office investment team.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. MOB (medical office building) sales in Grand Rapids do not signal residential demand shifts. However, the buyer's interest in below-market rent upside suggests general distress in secondary-market CRE and conservative underwriting; multifamily developers in Midwest secondary markets should expect compressed cap rates and tighter underwriting on value-add and lease-up assumptions.

stories.title: Alliance for Downtown New York Inks 14K SF at 42 Broadway
stories.excerpt: Nonprofit group Alliance For Downtown New York has expanded its Lower Manhattan footprint to 42 Broadway. The Downtown Alliance, which manages the area’s business improvement district, secured a 14,420-square-foot lease at the Financial District tower, according to a recent CBRE office market report. The Downtown Alliance plans to relocate its operations division to the 22-story office building, a spokesperson for the nonprofit told CO. The nonprofit’s corporate headquarters remain housed roughly three blocks north at Silverstein Properties’ 120 Broadway. JLL’s John Wheeler and his team at JLL represented the tenant in the negotiations. A spokesperson for the team did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The lease terms were not disclosed, but office asking rents in Lower Manhattan averaged $61.91 per square foot in July, according to the CBRE report. A spokesperson for the landlord, Avi Schron‘s Cammeby’s International Group, confirmed the recent transaction to CO, adding that the space is still under construction. It was not immediately clear whether Cammeby’s International Group worked with any outside brokers. Cammeby’s 42 Broadway is located near the intersection of Broadway and Morris Street. Appellate service organization Office of the Appellate Defender relocated there in November, joining a tenant roster that includes office suite provider TKO Suites, chiropractor Prestige Health and Wellness, dental practice DDS Group and cafe Gregorys Coffee. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Alliance for Downtown New York leases 14.4K SF at 42 Broadway in Lower Manhattan Financial District.
Nonprofit relocating operations division; headquarters remain at 120 Broadway (Silverstein Properties).
Lower Manhattan office asking rents averaged $61.91/sf as of July 2024.
stories.summary: The Alliance for Downtown New York, the area's business improvement district, secured a 14,420-sf lease at 42 Broadway (Cammeby's International Group) to relocate its operations division while maintaining headquarters at Silverstein's 120 Broadway. JLL represented the nonprofit tenant. Office asking rents in Lower Manhattan averaged $61.91 per square foot as of July 2024.
stories.impact: Nonprofit institutional tenant leasing in Lower Manhattan signals sustained demand from quasi-governmental and service-sector anchors, but modest asking rents ($61.91/sf) reflect ongoing softness in secondary Financial District office. Multifamily developers should recognize that BID-anchored neighborhoods attract city workers and service employees; proximity to major office clusters can support mid-market rental housing in nearby precincts, but relative office weakness may limit income-driven renter migration into Lower Manhattan residential.

stories.title: New York’s Rent Freeze Was Only An Aftershock. This 2019 Law Was The Quake.
stories.excerpt: Jose Tur owns two rent-stabilized rental buildings in Manhattan’s Washington Heights with a total of 45 units. The properties have been in his family for over 30 years, and the mortgages are fully paid off. But Tur tells Commercial Observer that despite this, while he’s reluctant to give an exact number, “more than two or three” units have been sitting empty for an average of over two years. That’s because, according to Tur’s estimates, it would cost anywhere from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit to return them to a livable state, and that’s money he can’t justify spending in return for the stabilized rent amounts in today’s environment. “Some of them require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Tur, who has testified about these financial challenges to New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). “[Oftentimes] the plumbing’s really old because a tenant has lived there for 10 to 15 years, and you have to do the electrical and then lead abatement, which really increases the tally on the job.” Tur says that the $30,000 estimate is before taking into account more cosmetic fixes like cabinets, tiles and so forth, meaning the total is often closer to $60,000 for a one-bedroom apartment. Given all this, the fate of his currently empty apartments is uncertain. With no financial relief in sight, it is likely the units will not be lived in again for the foreseeable future, removed from the rolls of New York’s livable spaces — and from Tur’s income-producing properties — as if they had never existed. The RGB approved a freeze on rent increases for one- and two-year leases for the city’s rent-stabilized apartments in June for lease terms beginning on Oct. 1 or later. bullets: New York 2019 rent-stabilization law caps landlord returns; Washington Heights owner has 2–3+ vacant stabilized units.
Vacancy driven by $30K–$60K rehab costs per unit vs. frozen stabilized rents; units vacant 2+ years.
Lead abatement, plumbing, electrical work inflate baseline costs; mortgages paid off but capital deployment uneconomic.
stories.summary: A Manhattan rent-stabilized landlord with a fully-owned, 45-unit portfolio in Washington Heights has left 2–3+ units vacant for over two years because the $30K–$60K per-unit renovation cost (baseline plumbing, electrical, lead abatement) cannot be justified against frozen stabilized rents. The 2019 rent-stabilization law constrains landlord returns, and even debt-free ownership cannot overcome the rent-cap economics that render capital redeployment irrational.
stories.impact: New York's 2019 rent-regulation law creates long-term reduction in stabilized housing supply as landlords rationally withdraw units rather than reinvest. Multifamily developers should expect continued decay and abandonment of mid-stock rent-stabilized buildings in outer boroughs (Washington Heights, upper Manhattan); this simultaneously reduces primary supply and signals a durable market gap for well-capitalized, market-rate development targeting displaced renters willing to pay for maintained, modern units. Window to acquire and reposition distressed stabilized buildings for market-rate conversion is tightening as city enforcement and vacancy penalties increase.

stories.title: Local Developer Plans to Build a School at 1000 University Avenue in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: School is in session in the Bronx, or at least it will be. Kiumarz Geula, principal of real estate development firm Pillar Property Management, has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to build a seven-story school building at 1000 University Avenue in the Highbridge neighborhood of the Bronx. The plans were filed with the DOB on Aug. 5. Geula did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Jonathan Imani of IMC Architecture, the registered architect on the project, also did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. The DOB plans have few details about the scope of the work coming to the vacant Bronx property. The plans call for the construction of a 64,366-square-foot, 108-foot tall building with a cafeteria and recreation space. No other details are available. Pillar Property Management isn’t the only developer planning to bring a new school building to the Bronx. In June, Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures secured a $60 million debt package to acquire and build a charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue, Commercial Observer reported at the time. Ripco Real Estate’s James Murad, who arranged the financing for that deal, told CO at the time that the project reflects “the growing demand for high-quality educational facilities in underserved communities and the continued appeal of mission-driven real estate investments.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Pillar Property Management filed plans with NYC DOB to build seven-story school at 1000 University Ave, Bronx.
64.4K SF building, 108 feet tall; cafeteria and recreation space; filed Aug. 5, 2024.
Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures also building charter school at 1780 East Tremont Ave, Bronx ($60M debt).
stories.summary: Pillar Property Management has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings to construct a 64,366-sf, seven-story school building at 1000 University Avenue in the Highbridge neighborhood of the Bronx. The 108-foot-tall building will include cafeteria and recreation space. This follows a separate $60M debt financing for Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures' charter school project at 1780 East Tremont Avenue in the Bronx.
stories.impact: Surge in new school construction in the Bronx signals sustained population growth and family formation in outer-borough neighborhoods, particularly in education-constrained communities. Multifamily developers should view school and institutional facility investment as a leading indicator of neighborhood stabilization and family-renter demand in the Bronx; increased school capacity can unlock migration from Manhattan and nearby districts, supporting both market-rate and affordable housing demand in Highbridge and East Tremont submarkets.
